title: Control procurement, decanting and storage
audience: Any worker in any home-service business, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish the documented requirements for procurement and storage from unsupported product claims.
Demonstrate correct verify–authorise–record–escalate decisions for a customer worksite.
Describe when local legislation, product labelling or specialist review governs the task.
Explain the applicable limits and safeguards for control procurement, decanting and storage.

instruction.heading: Why control starts before the product arrives
instruction.body: Many chemical problems in cleaning businesses trace back to a product nobody can identify: a drum with no label, a bottle decanted into a drink container, a supplier substitute sold under the old nickname, or incompatible products stored side by side. This lesson covers how to control what you buy, how to transfer product safely from bulk containers to working containers, and how to store stock so that a worker can always tell what it is, what it is for and what to do if it spills. Procurement and storage are not paperwork. They are the controls that make a product safe to use.

instruction.heading: Procure only approved products
instruction.body: Keep an approved products register that records, for each product, the supplier, the product name and version, the formulation or composition reference, the SDS date, the approved uses and the storage requirements. A product is bought only if it is on the register or has been added after review. When a delivery arrives, check its label and SDS against the register and the order. A new formulation sold under an old name is a different product until it has been reviewed, because the nickname on an order is not evidence of identity. Hold any stock that does not match, and do not release it to a worker until the SDS, the label and the compatibility review have been completed and recorded. Ask the supplier to notify you of formulation changes in writing.

instruction.heading: Decant only into suitable, labelled containers
instruction.body: Decanting is a transfer, and every transfer is a chance for a mistake. Use only containers that are clean, undamaged, compatible with the product and designated for chemicals. Never decant into a food or drink container, a bottle that has held food, or an unlabelled container. Label each working container with the product identifier, the main hazards from the SDS, the date of transfer and the initials of the person who made it. Measure the product with a graduated container or the approved dispensing system, follow the PPE and handling advice in the SDS, and never top up one product with another. Record each transfer, including any spill and how it was cleaned up. Where the label or SDS does not cover decanting, the transfer waits until a supervisor has checked it.

instruction.heading: Store stock so it can be identified and separated
instruction.body: Store products closed, labelled and upright where the label requires it, in a dedicated and ventilated area that is secure from unauthorised access. Separate products that the SDS says are incompatible, and keep acids, alkalis and oxidisers apart from each other and from other products where the SDS directs. Keep chemicals away from food, and keep working containers where the person using them can see the label. Check the storage area regularly for leaks, damaged or bulging containers, corroded lids and missing labels. Where expiry or supplier guidance applies, rotate stock so the oldest product is used first. A damaged or unidentified container is isolated, recorded, and its disposal is referred to a competent person under local rules.

instruction.heading: Count and record the stock
instruction.body: Run a stock check at a set interval, recording the stock on hand, the expiry dates, any damaged containers and any product found without a label. Compare the count with the register and recent purchases, and investigate any difference you cannot explain. A product with no SDS on file is a control failure, and it is withdrawn from use until the file is complete. The check is also the moment to confirm that working containers are labelled and that the approved products list is current.

instruction.heading: Worked check on a supplier substitute
instruction.body: Suppose a supplier substitutes a differently formulated concentrate under the same informal product nickname. The new drum looks like the old one and the order uses the same name. The correct decision is to hold the new stock and not release it. Request the fresh SDS, the new label and the composition, and check them against the register and the compatibility guidance for the surfaces the product will be used on. Record the substitution in the register, withdraw any working container of the new product until it has been reviewed, and tell the supervisor. Release the stock only after the review is recorded and the approved uses are updated.

instruction.heading: Legal limits of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson does not authorise the purchase, transport, storage or use of any regulated product. Check the label, the SDS and the employer's approved products list, and follow the local rules for disposing of residues.

instruction.heading: Stop-work rule
instruction.body: Stop and tell your supervisor before using or moving a product if its identity cannot be confirmed, if its label or SDS is missing or damaged, if you find an unlabelled or leaking container, if a product has been put into a food or drink container, if incompatible products are stored together, or if you are asked to use stock that has not been released. Isolate the container, keep people away from any spill, and do not pour it into another container.

procedure: Check every product against the approved products register before it is ordered, and record any new product for review.
On delivery, check the label, the SDS and the order against the register, and hold any mismatch.
Record the SDS date, the formulation reference and the approved uses on the register for each released product.
Decant only into clean, designated containers, and never into food or drink containers.
Label each working container with the product identifier, the main hazards, the date and the initials of the person who made the transfer.
Store products closed, labelled, upright where required, and separated by incompatibility according to the SDS.
Rotate stock so the oldest product is used first where expiry or supplier guidance requires it.
Run the stock check at a set interval, and record stock on hand, expiry dates, damaged containers and unlabelled products.

workedExamples.situation: A supplier substitutes a differently formulated concentrate under the same informal product nickname.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first safe action, and who must be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: The first safe action is to hold the new stock so it is not released or decanted. Request the fresh SDS, label and composition, and compare them with the register and the surface guidance. Tell the supervisor and record the substitution. Do not treat the old nickname as proof the product is the same. Release happens only after the review is recorded.

workedExamples.situation: A worker finds an unlabelled bottle of working solution on a shelf next to the food storage area, and nobody remembers who made it.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the worker use it because it looks like the usual product?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The contents are unknown, so the identity, hazards and approved uses cannot be confirmed. The worker isolates the bottle away from food, keeps people away from it, tells the supervisor and records its location. It is not used or poured into another container. A competent person decides, under the local rules, whether it can be identified or must be disposed of.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence notice: completing this lesson is not a licence, certificate or authority to do regulated or restricted work. Check the licence or authorisation rules for your state or territory, and obtain your employer or site written authorisation before starting any work that is outside your training.

Stop-work rule: stop, make the area safe and tell your supervisor before continuing if the task is outside your training or authorisation, the hazard or the required permission is unclear, or the client asks for work that the work order does not cover.

qualityStandard: Only products on the approved register, or products reviewed and added to it, are bought and released.
Each delivery's label and SDS are checked against the register and the order, and mismatched stock is held.
Decanting uses only clean, labelled, designated containers, never a food or drink container.
Products are stored closed, labelled and separated by incompatibility, and stock checks record expiry dates, damage and unlabelled product.
summary: Buy and release only products that are on the approved register or have been reviewed.
A product nickname does not prove identity; check the label, the SDS and the composition against the register.
Decant only into clean, labelled, designated containers, never into food or drink containers.
Store products closed, labelled and separated by incompatibility according to the SDS, and away from food.
Run stock checks that record expiry dates, damage and unlabelled product, and withdraw anything that cannot be identified.

knowledgeChecks.question: What must you verify before proceeding with procurement and storage?
options: That the decanted container looks the same as before, and that it is in a clean bottle at the store today
That the product nickname matches the one on the last order, and the price is the same as before
That the supplier's price is the lowest on the market and the delivery is the fastest available
The exact product and formulation delivered, checked against its documented requirements, not just its nickname

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the approved products register record for each product?
options: The supplier, the product name and version, the formulation reference, the SDS date, the approved uses and the storage requirements
